We know that, the nth term of a G.P. with first term a and common ratio r is tn=arn-1.

Then, b=ar and c=ar2

Now, 3a, 7b and 15c are in A.P.

⇒14b=3a+15c

⇒14ar=3a+15(ar2)

⇒14r=3+15r2

⇒15r2-14r+3=0

⇒3r-15r-3=0

⇒r=13 or  r=35

The only acceptable value is r=13, because r∈0, 12

∴ the first term of the A.P. is A=3a and the common difference is d=7b-3a=7ar-3a=73a-3a=-23a

Also, we know that the nth term of an A.P. with first term A and common difference d is Tn=A+n-1d

∴ T4=3a+4-1-23a= 3a-2a=a.

questions.q: The number of terms of an A.P. is even; the sum of all the odd terms is 24 , the sum of all the even terms is 30 and the last term exceeds the first by $\frac{21}{2}$. Then the number of terms which are integers in the A.P. is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{a}_2+\mathrm{a}_4+\ldots+\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{n}}=30$ ...(1)
$\mathrm{a}_1+\mathrm{a}_3+\ldots+\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{n}-1}=24$ ...(2)
$(1)-(2)$
$\left(a_2-a_1\right)+\left(a_4-a_3\right) \ldots\left(a_n-a_{n-1}\right)=6$
$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{n}}{2} \mathrm{~d}=6 \Rightarrow \mathrm{nd}=12 \\ & \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{n}}-\mathrm{a}_1=(\mathrm{n}-1) \mathrm{d}=\frac{21}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{nd}-\mathrm{d}=\frac{21}{2} \Rightarrow 12-\frac{21}{2}=\mathrm{d} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{d}=\frac{3}{2}, \mathrm{n}=8\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}
& \text { Sum of odd terms }=\frac{4}{2}[2 \mathrm{a}+(4-1) 3]=24 \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=\frac{3}{2} \\ & \text { A.P. } \Rightarrow \frac{3}{2}, 3, \frac{9}{2}, 6, \frac{15}{2}, 9, \frac{21}{2}, 12
\end{aligned}$
no. of integer terms $=4$

questions.solution:
Let the common difference of an A.P. be d, then

a1+a2+a3+a4=50

⇒4a+6d=50

⇒32+6d=50

⇒d=3

Also,

an-3+an-2+an-1+an=170

⇒4a+4n-10·d=170

⇒32+4n-10·3=170

⇒n=14

So, middle terms are 

a7=a+6d=26, a8=a+7d=29

⇒a7·a8=754

questions.q: If the arithmetic mean and the geometric mean of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>th</mi></msup></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>q</mi><mi>th</mi></msup></math> terms of the sequence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>-</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>-</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>…</mo></math> satisfy the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><mn>9</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi></math> is equal to _______.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let tp & tq is the pth & qth terms of the series -16,8,-4,2,...

Here a=-16, r=-12

Then, tp=-16-12p-1

tq=-16-12q-1

The roots of the given quadratic equation 4x2-9x+5=0 is x=1,54. 

AM=54, GM=1 ∵AM≥GM

Now, given 54=tp+tq2,1=tptq

So, 1=256-12p+q-2⇒2p+q-2=-1p+q-228

⇒2p+q-10=-1p+q-2

It is equal when 2p+q-10=1=-1p+q-2

Hence, p+q-10=0⇒p+q=10

questions.q: The number of 3 -digit numbers, that are divisible by 2 and 3 , but not divisible by 4 and 9 , is______.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
No, of 3 digits $=999-99=900$
No. of 3 digit numbers divisible by 2 & 3 i.e. by 6
$\frac{900}{6}=150$

No. of 3 digit numbers divisible by 4 & 9 i.e. by 36
$\frac{900}{36}=25\therefore$ No of 3 digit numbers divisible by $2 ~\&~ 3$ but not by $4 ~\&~ 9150-25=125$
